description: I am an electronic engineer participating individually in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. My background includes hardware design, microcontroller programming, signal analysis, and systems integration. As a solo team, I take on every role—research, development, documentation, and presentation—which pushes me to be efficient, prioritize effectively, and learn quickly. I bring genuine enthusiasm, technical discipline, and the drive to contribute a meaningful solution to this global challenge.
summary:
Outpost Neurodiverso is a bilingual browser game for kids aged 7–12. The player runs a Moon base by sharing 4 units of solar power among shield, air, greenhouse and lab, while real solar events recorded by NASA DONKI arrive. Every decision has a cost: reinforcing the shield uses power you need for air; resting costs a mission day.

The project comes from my experience as an engineer with ADHD. Instead of adding accessibility at the end, cognitive diversity is part of the rules: the crew's mental energy shows on their faces, and the player chooses among four processing "superpowers" (Quick eye, Planner, Narrator, Forecaster), each with a real in-game cost. There is no "normal" mode, no time limit, and failure is never framed as punishment but as a mission report.

It matters because it teaches two things at once: that no space engineering decision is free, and that managing your own way of processing also has strategy.
details:
What it does and how it works
I made a bilingual (English and Spanish) browser game for kids aged 7–12. The player runs a Moon base by sharing 4 units of solar power among four modules: shield, air, greenhouse and lab. Every tap changes something visible right away: the shield grows, the air tank fills, the plant sprouts. When the day ends, the night resolves everything without randomness: the crew breathes, eats, rests or gets tired. Every 3 days a real solar event from NASA's DONKI database arrives. If it is a particle storm and the shield is too low, air and the crew's mental energy drop. The player can earn up to 3 stars: survive every day, collect 3 science samples and block every storm. Each event survived becomes a collectible card with a link to its official page on NASA's website.

Benefits and the impact I am looking for
The game teaches two layers of decisions at once. The first is space engineering: power is limited and must be split among life support, shielding, food and research; no decision is free. The second is neurodivergent: the crew's mental energy is a visible resource shown on their faces, and the player chooses among four processing "superpowers" (Quick eye, Planner, Narrator, Forecaster), each with a real in-game cost. There is no "normal" mode, no time limit, no flashing, and failure is never framed as punishment but as a mission report with a reflective question. What I am looking for is that neurodivergent kids (autistic, with ADHD and other ways of processing) can play without feeling out of place, and that any child understands that managing their own way of processing is also a strategy. The design follows the three principles of Universal Design for Learning (CAST, UDL 3.0).

Tools, languages and software I used
I used HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks or dependencies. Data is stored in a local JSON file with a built-in fallback, so the game works offline. There is no backend, no accounts, no downloads. It is published on GitHub Pages and runs on computers, tablets and phones. Real data comes from NASA's public DONKI API (FLR, SEP and CME endpoints) and NASA's OSDR repository. The Canadian Space Agency educational toolkit framed the food-production section. I developed the code, texts and balance simulations with assistance from generative AI (Claude, by Anthropic), under my direction, review and testing.

What makes it creative
The creative part is turning neurodiversity into mechanics, not accessibility added at the end. The "superpowers" are not difficulty modes: they are ways of processing with real costs inside the simulation. Mental energy shows on the crew's faces, not in an abstract number. The album of real solar-event cards turns each playthrough into a verifiable collection with links to NASA's official website. And failure is presented as a mission report, not as a "you lost" screen.

Factors I considered
I thought about the target age (7–12): simple language and scientific terms explained in context. I took care of cognitive accessibility: minimum 18 px text, large buttons, colors always paired with icons or words, no harsh animations, optional sound off by default, and compatibility with keyboard, mouse and touch. I also took care of data honesty: historical events are clearly labeled as historical and live events as live; I did not use RadLab because its server returned HTTP 500 during development, and I wrote that in the README. For balance I simulated 4,000 games per strategy and superpower, and verified the game can be won without reacting fast, reading fast or guessing hidden rules. Finally, I made sure the game never names diagnoses or asks the player to identify themselves.
